title: Anansi the Blind Fisherman
subtitle: Kind helpers meet an ungrateful response

learningObjectives.text: How do the two men help Anansi before the final trip?
Why does Anansi jump into deep water?

fisherman.author: W. H. Barker and Cecilia Sinclair
fisherman.translator: not applicable; collected, arranged, and retold in English
fisherman.locator: Story XI · ANANSI THE BLIND FISHERMAN; Story XI · ANANSI THE BLIND FISHERMAN, normalized characters 650-2204
fisherman.excerpt: When they told him where to spread his net, he would reply sharply, “I know. I was just about to put it there.” When they were directing him to get out of the boat, he would say, “Oh, I know perfectly well we are at the beach. I was just getting ready to step out.” This went on for a long time, Anansi getting ruder and ruder to his helpers every day, until they could bear his treatment no longer. They determined when opportunity offered to punish him for his ingratitude. The next day, as usual, he came with them to the beach. When they had got the canoe ready, they bade him step in. “Do you think I am a fool?” said he. “I know the canoe is there.” They made no answer, but got in and patiently pulled toward the fishing-place. When they told him where to spread his net, he replied with so much abuse that they determined, there and then, to punish him. By this time the canoe was full of fish, so they turned to row home. When they had gone a little way they stopped and said to him, “Here we are at the beach.” He promptly told them that they were very foolish—to tell him a thing he knew so well. He added many rude and insulting remarks, which made them thoroughly angry. He then jumped proudly out, expecting to land on the beach. To his great astonishment he found himself sinking in deep water. The two men rowed quickly away, leaving him to struggle. Like all the men of that country he was a good swimmer, but, of course, being blind, he was unable to see where the land lay. So he swam until he was completely tired out—and was drowned.
fisherman.note: Verbatim text from Barker and Sinclair's 1917 English collection of Gold Coast stories. Attribute any specific community only where the collection does so.

narrativeBlocks.title: Two helpers assist an old fisherman
narrativeBlocks.body: In Barker and Sinclair's tale, two men guide the blind Anansi into a canoe, help him fish, and lead him back to shore.

narrativeBlocks.title: Anansi refuses their help
narrativeBlocks.body: The men say the canoe has reached the beach. Anansi insists he knows where he is, jumps out, and finds himself in deep water.

narrativeBlocks.title: A specific Gold Coast collection
narrativeBlocks.body: This tale is one of Barker and Sinclair's 1917 Gold Coast folk-story collection. The book's introduction explains that versions were collected and retold; it does not identify this story's exact community.

narrativeBlocks.title: The story punishes ingratitude
narrativeBlocks.body: The tale links Anansi's insults to his helpers' decision to leave him; it is a literary moral, not a general statement about Akan or Gold Coast people.
